result.title: Canonical Correlation Neural Networks
result.summary: Relational inductive biases such as grids or graphs allow neural networks with fewer trainable parameters and improved generalization, but require a known structure beforehand. When no structure is available, the covariance matrix provides a principled substitute, and coVariance Neural Networks (VNNs) have shown that using it yields models that are theoretically grounded in Principal Component Analysis, stable to finite-sample estimation errors and parameter-efficient. This framework, however, is limited to single-view data, whereas many applications observe the same phenomenon through multiple views, each with its own in-view covariance and a cross-view covariance linking them. To incorporate these matrices as inductive biases in a principled way, we introduce CAnonical correlation NEural networks (CANEs), architectures that use in-view and cross-view covariances as distinct relational biases to solve downstream tasks. Via spectral analysis, CANEs draw analogies with Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA), a classical technique to project two-view data onto a correlated subspace. However, while CCA's objective is to compute shared view representations, CANEs are trained to solve a downstream task directly. We bound their output error under finite-sample covariance perturbations and show that it depends on controllable Lipschitz constants of the learned filters in place of the singular-value gap that governs the stability of CCA, thus guaranteeing better robustness. Experiments on seven datasets from brain imaging and motion sensing show that CANEs match or outperform single-view, two-view and CCA-based baselines, often with fewer parameters, and retain their performance when covariances are re-estimated from fewer samples.

AI.brief_summary: 该文提出 CANE，把单视图内的协方差与视图间的交叉协方差作为两种关系归纳偏置，在谱域构造参数高效的多视图网络，并给出有限样本协方差扰动下的输出误差界，在脑成像与运动传感数据上验证。
AI.relevance_reason: 其用交叉协方差与谱滤波对齐两个视图并抵抗估计噪声的做法，可能为 LVR 中视觉证据与 latent 状态的对齐、融合及表示稳定性提供可核查的架构线索，但需确认迁移是否超出线性二阶统计的适用条件。
